title: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Active Setup
shortTitle: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Active Setup
summary: Active Setup is a Windows mechanism that runs configured programs after a user signs in, and it exists originally to complete per-user parts of a software installation. Each component is described by a subkey under the Active Setup installed components path, and the StubPath value names the command to run. An adversary creates a component key, points StubPath at their payload, and Windows runs it in the context of the user who logs on, with that account's permissions. Because the mechanism tracks completion per user, the command runs once for each account on the host, which spreads execution across everyone who signs in and makes the behaviour look like ordinary software setup work. Detection focuses on that registry path: new component keys, especially ones whose identifiers do not match a known product, and StubPath values that point outside normal program directories. Correlating registry writes with process creation shortly after logon confirms the mechanism is being used.

beginner.definition: Active Setup is a Windows feature that runs setup tasks after a person signs in. It exists so software can finish preparing itself for each user. An attacker can add a task of their own, so their program runs each time someone logs on.
beginner.whyItMatters: The program runs with the permissions of the user who signs in, so no extra password prompt appears. It runs once for each account on the computer, which means it can spread across all the people who use the machine. The settings live in the registry under a name that sounds like normal software installation work. Most people never open that part of the registry, so the change can remain for a long time.
howItWorks: Windows keeps a set of Active Setup components in a registry key for the whole computer.
Each component has its own subkey and a value that names the command to run.
When a user signs in, Windows checks which components have not yet run for that account.
It runs the command from the value and then records that the component is complete for that user.
An attacker creates a component key and points the command value at their own program.
Detection looks for new component keys and commands that sit outside normal program folders.
beginner.example: Think of a library that lends out reading lamps. When a new member joins, the desk clerk checks a list of jobs and switches on the lamps that member needs. Someone adds a job to the list that says switch on the side door. Every new member causes the clerk to unlock that door, and the clerk assumes the job came from the library manager.
takeaways: Active Setup runs once per user, so a single registry change can affect every account on the host.
Review that registry path for component keys that do not belong to known software.
Check the command named in each component, and be suspicious of paths in user folders or temporary areas.

objectives: Explain what Active Setup is and why Windows runs these components after logon.
Identify the registry path that stores Active Setup components and the value that names the command.
Describe how the per-user completion record makes a component run once for every account.
Detect suspicious Active Setup components using registry monitoring and logon process correlation.
Explain how masquerading makes a malicious component resemble legitimate installation work.
Explain how this sub-technique differs from logon scripts and other Windows autostart methods.
